    mixed_cage_order 1 z g ≤ if Even z then z * (g - 1) + 2 else (z + 1) * (g - 1)
open.citation: arXiv:2610.14110 (New mixed cages, bounds and computational results), Theorem 4.2 (with Definition 4.1).

open.name: nonsustainable_tree_has_nonsustainable_successor_closer_to_star
open.informal: Every non-sustainable tree X on Fin n (n ≥ 2) that is not isomorphic to the star completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n-1)) has a non-sustainable generalized-tree-shift successor Y whose adjacency spectral radius is strictly larger.
open.statement:
theorem nonsustainable_tree_has_nonsustainable_successor_closer_to_star
    (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) (X : SimpleGraph (Fin n))
    (hX : is_nonsustainable_tree X)
    (hXs : ¬ Nonempty (X ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)))) :
    ∃ Y : SimpleGraph (Fin n),
      is_nonsustainable_tree Y ∧ is_generalized_tree_shift X Y ∧
      adjacency_spectral_radius X < adjacency_spectral_radius Y

open.name: odd_antihole_colorable_of_common_palette
open.informal: Theorem 8 of arXiv:2610.14241 for the odd antihole: for ℓ ≥ 3, if all lists of an (ℓ-1)-assignment of complement(C_{2ℓ-1}) are subsets of a common ℓ-set P and are not all identical, then the antihole is L-colorable.
open.statement:
theorem odd_antihole_colorable_of_common_palette (ℓ : ℕ) (hℓ : 3 ≤ ℓ) (P : Finset ℕ)
    (hP : P.card = ℓ) (L : Fin (2 * ℓ - 1) → Finset ℕ) (hL : ∀ v, (L v).card = ℓ - 1)
    (hLP : ∀ v, L v ⊆ P) (hne : ∃ u v, L u ≠ L v) :
    ∃ c : Fin (2 * ℓ - 1) → ℕ, (∀ v, c v ∈ L v) ∧
      ∀ u v, (SimpleGraph.cycleGraph (2 * ℓ - 1))ᶜ.Adj u v → c u ≠ c v
open.citation: arXiv:2610.14241 (Restricting odd antiholes in critical graphs via list coloring), Theorem 8, specialized to G = complement of C_{2ℓ-1} (whose complement, the odd cycle, is hypomatchable); partial result for OP-216 (the conjecture with the common-palette assumption)

open.name: odd_antihole_strongly_chromatic_choosable
open.informal: Conjecture 9 of arXiv:2610.14241: for every integer ℓ ≥ 3, the odd antihole, the complement of the cycle C_{2ℓ-1}, is strongly ℓ-chromatic-choosable: it has chromatic number ℓ, and for every assignment of lists of size ℓ-1 to its vertices that are not all the same list, it has a proper coloring from the lists.
open.statement:
theorem odd_antihole_strongly_chromatic_choosable (ℓ : ℕ) (hℓ : 3 ≤ ℓ) :
    IsStronglyChromaticChoosable (SimpleGraph.cycleGraph (2 * ℓ - 1))ᶜ ℓ
open.citation: arXiv:2610.14241 (Restricting odd antiholes in critical graphs via list coloring), Conjecture 9 (open; the cases ℓ = 3 and ℓ = 4 are known, ℓ = 5 is the first case with new consequences, and Theorem 8 proves it when all lists lie in a common ℓ-set)

open.name: op223_adjacency_spectral_radius_iso
open.informal: The adjacency spectral radius is an isomorphism invariant of finite simple graphs: if G and H are isomorphic finite simple graphs then their adjacency spectral radii are equal.
open.statement:
theorem op223_adjacency_spectral_radius_iso {V W : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    [Fintype W] [DecidableEq W]
    {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W} (e : G ≃g H) :
    adjacency_spectral_radius G = adjacency_spectral_radius H

open.name: op223_is_sustainable_tree_iso_invariant
open.informal: For isomorphic finite simple graphs G and H, G is a sustainable tree if and only if H is.
open.statement:
theorem op223_is_sustainable_tree_iso_invariant {V W : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    [Fintype W] [DecidableEq W] {G : SimpleGraph V} {H : SimpleGraph W} (e : G ≃g H) :
    is_sustainable_tree G ↔ is_sustainable_tree H

open.name: op223_nonsustainable_tree_fin_four
open.informal: Every non-sustainable tree on four vertices is isomorphic to the star graph K_{1,3}.
open.statement:
theorem op223_nonsustainable_tree_fin_four (X : SimpleGraph (Fin 4))
    (hX : is_nonsustainable_tree X) :
    Nonempty (X ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3))

open.name: op223_path_four_radius_le_seventeen_tenths
open.informal: The adjacency spectral radius of the path on four vertices is at most 17/10.
open.statement:
theorem op223_path_four_radius_le_seventeen_tenths :
    adjacency_spectral_radius (SimpleGraph.pathGraph 4) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal ((17 : ℝ) / 10)

open.name: op223_sqrt_three_le_star_three_radius
open.informal: The adjacency spectral radius of the star K_{1,3} is at least sqrt 3.
open.statement:
theorem op223_sqrt_three_le_star_three_radius :
    ENNReal.ofReal (Real.sqrt 3) ≤
      adjacency_spectral_radius (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3))

open.name: op223_star_adjacency_spectral_radius
open.informal: The adjacency spectral radius of the star K_{1,n-1} (as completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n-1))) is sqrt(n-1), for n >= 2.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_adjacency_spectral_radius (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) :
    adjacency_spectral_radius (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))) =
      ENNReal.ofReal (Real.sqrt ((n : ℝ) - 1))

open.name: op223_star_edge_swap_radius_lt
open.informal: If S is a star K_{1,n-1} on n >= 4 vertices, e is an edge of S, f a non-edge of S, and deleting e and adding f yields a tree, then that tree has strictly smaller adjacency spectral radius than S.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_edge_swap_radius_lt {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (S : SimpleGraph V)
    (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n)
    (hS : Nonempty (S ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))))
    (e : Sym2 V) (he : e ∈ S.edgeSet) (f : Sym2 V) (hf : f ∈ Sᶜ.edgeSet)
    (htree : (S.deleteEdges {e} ⊔ SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f}).IsTree) :
    adjacency_spectral_radius (S.deleteEdges {e} ⊔ SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f}) <
      adjacency_spectral_radius S

open.name: op223_star_is_nonsustainable
open.informal: For any natural number n ≥ 4 and any simple graph S on a finite vertex type V, if S is isomorphic to the star graph completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)), then S is a non-sustainable tree.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_is_nonsustainable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (S : SimpleGraph V) (n : ℕ) (_hn : 4 ≤ n)
    (hS : Nonempty (S ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)))) :
    is_nonsustainable_tree S

open.name: op223_star_like_edgeSet_nonempty
open.informal: A finite simple graph S isomorphic to the star K_{1,n-1} with n >= 4 has at least one edge.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_like_edgeSet_nonempty {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (S : SimpleGraph V) (n : ℕ)
    (hn : 4 ≤ n) (hS : Nonempty (S ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)))) :
    ∃ e, e ∈ S.edgeSet

open.name: op223_star_like_is_tree
open.informal: Any finite simple graph S isomorphic to the star K_{1,n-1} with n >= 2 is a tree.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_like_is_tree {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (S : SimpleGraph V) (n : ℕ)
    (hn : 2 ≤ n) (hS : Nonempty (S ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)))) :
    S.IsTree

open.name: op223_star_swap_radius_lt_canonical
open.informal: At the canonical star K_{1,n-1} with n >= 4, moving leaf b off the centre (Sum.inl 0) and onto a different leaf m (i.e. deleting {centre, b} and adding {b, m}) strictly decreases the adjacency spectral radius.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_swap_radius_lt_canonical (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n) (b m : Fin (n - 1)) (hbm : b ≠ m) :
    adjacency_spectral_radius
      ((completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))).deleteEdges {s(Sum.inl 0, Sum.inr b)} ⊔
        SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {s(Sum.inr b, Sum.inr m)}) <
    adjacency_spectral_radius (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)))

open.name: op223_star_swap_structure
open.informal: At the canonical star K_{1,n-1} with n >= 4, if e is an edge and f a non-edge such that deleting e and adding f yields a tree, then e joins the centre to some leaf b and f joins that same leaf b to a different leaf m.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_swap_structure (n : ℕ) (hn : 4 ≤ n)
    (e f : Sym2 (Fin 1 ⊕ Fin (n - 1)))
    (he : e ∈ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))).edgeSet)
    (hf : f ∈ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)))ᶜ.edgeSet)
    (htree : ((completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))).deleteEdges {e} ⊔ SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f}).IsTree) :
    ∃ (b m : Fin (n - 1)), b ≠ m ∧ e = s(Sum.inl 0, Sum.inr b) ∧ f = s(Sum.inr b, Sum.inr m)

open.name: op223_star_swap_transport
open.informal: Transporting an edge-swap at a star along an isomorphism: if S is isomorphic to the star K_{1,n-1}, and e is an edge, f a non-edge, with S - e + f a tree, then there are an edge e' and non-edge f' of the canonical star such that the canonical swap is again a tree and the swap graphs S - e + f and star - e' + f' are isomorphic.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_swap_transport {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (S : SimpleGraph V) (n : ℕ)
    (hS : Nonempty (S ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))))
    (e f : Sym2 V) (he : e ∈ S.edgeSet) (hf : f ∈ Sᶜ.edgeSet)
    (htree : (S.deleteEdges {e} ⊔ SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f}).IsTree) :
    ∃ (e' f' : Sym2 (Fin 1 ⊕ Fin (n - 1))),
      e' ∈ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))).edgeSet ∧
      f' ∈ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1)))ᶜ.edgeSet ∧
      ((completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))).deleteEdges {e'} ⊔
          SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f'}).IsTree ∧
      Nonempty ((S.deleteEdges {e} ⊔ SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f}) ≃g
        ((completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin (n - 1))).deleteEdges {e'} ⊔
          SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f'}))

open.name: op223_star_three_not_sustainable
open.informal: Any finite simple graph isomorphic to the star K_{1,3} is not a sustainable tree.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_three_not_sustainable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (S : SimpleGraph V) (hS : Nonempty (S ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3))) :
    ¬ is_sustainable_tree S

open.name: op223_star_three_swap_yields_path
open.informal: At the canonical star K_{1,3}, if e is an edge and f a non-edge such that deleting e and adding f yields a tree, then the resulting tree is isomorphic to the path graph on four vertices.
open.statement:
theorem op223_star_three_swap_yields_path (e f : Sym2 (Fin 1 ⊕ Fin 3))
    (he : e ∈ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3)).edgeSet)
    (hf : f ∈ (completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3))ᶜ.edgeSet)
    (htree : ((completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3)).deleteEdges {e} ⊔
      SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f}).IsTree) :
    Nonempty (((completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3)).deleteEdges {e} ⊔
      SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {f}) ≃g SimpleGraph.pathGraph 4)

open.name: op223_sustainable_tree_fin_four
open.informal: Every sustainable tree on four vertices is isomorphic to the path graph on four vertices.
open.statement:
theorem op223_sustainable_tree_fin_four (X : SimpleGraph (Fin 4))
    (hX : is_sustainable_tree X) :
    Nonempty (X ≃g SimpleGraph.pathGraph 4)

open.name: op223_tree_fin_four_iso_path_or_star
open.informal: Every tree on four vertices is isomorphic either to the path graph on four vertices or to the star K_{1,3}.
open.statement:
theorem op223_tree_fin_four_iso_path_or_star (X : SimpleGraph (Fin 4)) (hX : X.IsTree) :
    Nonempty (X ≃g SimpleGraph.pathGraph 4) ∨
      Nonempty (X ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 1) (Fin 3))

open.name: op223_weighted_spectral_radius_bound
open.informal: Collatz–Wielandt / Gershgorin row-sum bound: if A is a real nonnegative matrix with zero diagonal and d is a strictly positive weight vector whose weighted row sums (1/d k) * sum_j A k j * d j are all at most R, then the spectral radius of A is at most R.
open.statement:
theorem op223_weighted_spectral_radius_bound {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] [Nonempty ι]
    (A : Matrix ι ι ℝ) (d : ι → ℝ) (hd : ∀ i, 0 < d i)
    (hdiag : ∀ i, A i i = 0) (hA : ∀ i j, 0 ≤ A i j)
    (R : ℝ) (hR : ∀ k, (1 / d k) * ∑ j, A k j * d j ≤ R) :
    spectralRadius ℝ A ≤ ENNReal.ofReal R

open.name: regular_tournament_arborescence_max_nearly_doubly_regular
open.informal: For every k >= 1, a regular tournament of order 4k+1 that maximizes the total number of arborescences tau among all regular tournaments of order 4k+1 is nearly doubly regular: every two distinct vertices have k-1 or k common out-neighbours.
open.statement:
theorem regular_tournament_arborescence_max_nearly_doubly_regular (k : ℕ) (hk : 1 ≤ k)
    (D : Digraph (Fin (4 * k + 1))) [DecidableRel D.Adj] (hD : digraph_is_tournament D)
    (hreg : ∀ v, digraph_out_count D v = 2 * k)
    (hmax : ∀ (D' : Digraph (Fin (4 * k + 1))) [DecidableRel D'.Adj],
      digraph_is_tournament D' → (∀ v, digraph_out_count D' v = 2 * k) →
      digraph_arborescence_count D' ≤ digraph_arborescence_count D) :
    ∀ i j, i ≠ j → digraph_common_out_count D i j = k - 1 ∨
      digraph_common_out_count D i j = k
open.citation: arXiv:2610.25886 (Extremal arborescences in graph orientations), Conjecture 6.1. The paper verifies it by computation for orders 5, 9, 13 and 17; at orders 3 mod 4 the maximizers are known to be doubly regular.

open.name: simple_graph_is_tree_stacking_number_eq_tree_estimate
open.informal: Conjecture: for every finite tree T, stack(T) = estim(T).
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_is_tree_stacking_number_eq_tree_estimate {V : Type*} [Fintype V]
    [DecidableEq V] (T : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel T.Adj] (hT : T.IsTree) :
    graph_stacking_number T = simple_graph_tree_estimate T
open.citation: arXiv:2610.09650 (The Almost Stacked Hypothesis: A Conjectural Analogue of Sjöstrand's Cover Pebbling Theorem), Conjecture 5.6. The paper proves stack(T) ≥ estim(T) unconditionally (Theorem 5.2) and the reverse inequality under the Almost Stacked Hypothesis (Theorem 5.4).

open.name: simple_graph_is_tree_tree_estimate_le_stacking_number
open.informal: For every finite tree T, stack(T) ≥ estim(T).
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_is_tree_tree_estimate_le_stacking_number {V : Type*} [Fintype V]
    [DecidableEq V] (T : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel T.Adj] (hT : T.IsTree) :
    simple_graph_tree_estimate T ≤ graph_stacking_number T
open.citation: arXiv:2610.09650 (The Almost Stacked Hypothesis: A Conjectural Analogue of Sjöstrand's Cover Pebbling Theorem), Theorem 5.2 (tree lower bound); one direction of Conjecture 5.6 (OP-144).

open.name: simple_graph_leap_group_card_odd_iff
open.informal: Let G be a finite simple graph that admits a hop. Then the leap group Λ₁(G) has odd order if and only if G is a disjoint union of cycles of odd length, i.e. G is 2-regular and every connected component has an odd number of vertices.
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_leap_group_card_odd_iff {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hG : ∃ h, simple_graph_is_hop G h) :
    Odd (Nat.card (simple_graph_leap_group G)) ↔
      (∀ v, G.degree v = 2) ∧ ∀ v, Odd (G.connectedComponentMk v).supp.ncard
open.citation: arXiv:2610.18463 (The group generated by a graph's derangements), Proposition 2.16. 'Disjoint union of odd-length cycles' is stated as: 2-regular with every connected component of odd order (a finite 2-regular simple graph is a disjoint union of cycles, each of length its component's order).

open.name: simple_graph_local_avg_dominating_order_stem_le
open.informal: Conjecture: if G is a graph of order n ≥ 2 without isolated vertices and v is an l-stem with l ≥ 1, then avd_v(G) ≤ (4n+1)/6, with equality if and only if l = 1 and G is star-like.
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_local_avg_dominating_order_stem_le {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]
    (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hn : 2 ≤ Fintype.card V)
    (hiso : ∀ w, 0 < G.degree w) (v : V) (hv : 1 ≤ simple_graph_leaf_neighbor_count G v) :
    simple_graph_local_avg_dominating_order G v ≤ (4 * (Fintype.card V : ℚ) + 1) / 6 ∧
      (simple_graph_local_avg_dominating_order G v = (4 * (Fintype.card V : ℚ) + 1) / 6 ↔
        simple_graph_leaf_neighbor_count G v = 1 ∧ simple_graph_is_star_like G)
open.citation: arXiv:2610.11446 (On the local average order of dominating sets), Conjecture 6.1. The paper proves the bound when every neighbour of v is a leaf or a stem (Theorem 5.2) and the strict bound for l ≥ 2 (Theorem 5.3); the open case is a 1-stem with a neighbour that is neither.

open.name: simple_graph_multi_radio_number_path_eventually
open.informal: For all k, m >= 1 there is n0 such that for every n >= n0 the (m,k)-radio number of the path P_n is ceil((k+1)^2/2) m - 1.
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_multi_radio_number_path_eventually :
    ∀ k m : ℕ, 1 ≤ k → 1 ≤ m → ∃ n₀ : ℕ, ∀ n, n₀ ≤ n →
      simple_graph_multi_radio_number (SimpleGraph.pathGraph n) m k =
        ((k + 1) ^ 2 + 1) / 2 * m - 1
open.citation: arXiv:2610.25863 (On Multi-label radio Labelings of Graphs), Conjecture 1; proved there for k = 1, 2, with the upper bound for k = 3 (Proposition 4.4)

open.name: simple_graph_multi_radio_number_path_three_of_le
open.informal: For every m >= 1 and every n >= 4m + 4, the (m,3)-radio number of the path P_n is exactly 8m - 1. This is the case k = 3 of Conjecture 1 of arXiv:2610.25863 with the explicit threshold n0 = 4m + 4.
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_multi_radio_number_path_three_of_le (n m : ℕ) (hm : 1 ≤ m)
    (hn : 4 * m + 4 ≤ n) :
    simple_graph_multi_radio_number (SimpleGraph.pathGraph n) m 3 = 8 * m - 1
open.citation: arXiv:2610.25863 (On Multi-label radio Labelings of Graphs), Conjecture 1 (case k = 3): the paper proves only the upper bound 8m - 1 (Proposition 4.4)

open.name: simple_graph_triangle_cover_number_le_two_mul_packing_number
open.informal: Tuza's conjecture: every finite simple graph G satisfies τ(G) ≤ 2ν(G).
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_triangle_cover_number_le_two_mul_packing_number :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)),
      simple_graph_triangle_cover_number G ≤ 2 * simple_graph_triangle_packing_number G
open.citation: arXiv:2610.15539 (Tuza's conjecture under an edge-count condition), Conjecture 1.1 (Tuza's conjecture, from 1981); the paper proves it for graphs with at least n²/4 − cn edges and large n, and the known general bound is τ ≤ (2.87…)ν. Stated for graphs on Fin n, which covers every finite graph up to isomorphism.

open.name: simple_graph_triangle_cover_number_le_two_mul_packing_number_of_max_degree_le_eleven
open.informal: Tuza's conjecture for graphs of maximum degree at most 11: every finite simple graph G with Δ(G) ≤ 11 satisfies τ(G) ≤ 2ν(G).
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_triangle_cover_number_le_two_mul_packing_number_of_max_degree_le_eleven :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj], (∀ v, G.degree v ≤ 11) →
      simple_graph_triangle_cover_number G ≤ 2 * simple_graph_triangle_packing_number G
open.citation: arXiv:2610.15269 (Tuza's Conjecture for Graphs of Maximum Degree at Most 10), Sec. 6: the next case after the paper's Theorem 1.1 (Δ ≤ 10).

open.name: simple_graph_triangle_cover_number_le_two_mul_packing_number_of_max_degree_le_ten
open.informal: Every finite simple graph G with maximum degree at most 10 satisfies τ(G) ≤ 2ν(G).
open.statement:
theorem simple_graph_triangle_cover_number_le_two_mul_packing_number_of_max_degree_le_ten :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj], (∀ v, G.degree v ≤ 10) →
      simple_graph_triangle_cover_number G ≤ 2 * simple_graph_triangle_packing_number G
open.citation: arXiv:2610.15269 (Tuza's Conjecture for Graphs of Maximum Degree at Most 10), Theorem 1.1; a special case of OP-207 and the base for OP-209.

open.name: subcubic_connected_ne_complete_four_exists_rich_neighbor_five_coloring
open.informal: Conjecture: every finite connected simple graph of maximum degree at most 3 other than K_4 admits a rich-neighbor 5-edge-colouring.
open.statement:
theorem subcubic_connected_ne_complete_four_exists_rich_neighbor_five_coloring {V : Type*}
    [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (hconn : G.Connected)
    (hdeg : G.maxDegree ≤ 3) (hK4 : IsEmpty (G ≃g (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 4)))) :
    ∃ c : G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin 5), simple_graph_is_rich_neighbor_coloring G c
open.citation: arXiv:2610.21868 (Rich-neighbor 5-edge-colorings of subcubic graphs whose 3-vertices induce a matching), Conjecture 1.1 (settled there when Δ(G[V_3]) ≤ 1, Theorem 1.2).

open.name: subcubic_three_vertices_max_degree_le_one_exists_rich_neighbor_five_coloring
open.informal: Every finite simple graph of maximum degree at most 3 in which each vertex of degree 3 has at most one neighbour of degree 3 (Δ(G[V_3]) ≤ 1) admits a rich-neighbor 5-edge-colouring.
open.statement:
theorem subcubic_three_vertices_max_degree_le_one_exists_rich_neighbor_five_coloring {V : Type*}
    [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hdeg : G.maxDegree ≤ 3)
    (h3 : ∀ v, G.degree v = 3 → ((G.neighborFinset v).filter (fun w => G.degree w = 3)).card ≤ 1) :
    ∃ c : G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin 5), simple_graph_is_rich_neighbor_coloring G c
open.citation: arXiv:2610.21868 (Rich-neighbor 5-edge-colorings of subcubic graphs whose 3-vertices induce a matching), Theorem 1.2.

open.name: subcubic_three_vertices_max_degree_le_two_exists_rich_neighbor_five_coloring
open.informal: Question: does every finite simple graph of maximum degree at most 3 in which each vertex of degree 3 has at most two neighbours of degree 3 (Δ(G[V_3]) ≤ 2) admit a rich-neighbor 5-edge-colouring?
open.statement:
theorem subcubic_three_vertices_max_degree_le_two_exists_rich_neighbor_five_coloring {V : Type*}
    [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hdeg : G.maxDegree ≤ 3)
    (h3 : ∀ v, G.degree v = 3 → ((G.neighborFinset v).filter (fun w => G.degree w = 3)).card ≤ 2) :
    ∃ c : G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin 5), simple_graph_is_rich_neighbor_coloring G c
open.citation: arXiv:2610.21868 (Rich-neighbor 5-edge-colorings of subcubic graphs whose 3-vertices induce a matching), Sec. 4 (next case after Theorem 1.2, which settles Δ(G[V_3]) ≤ 1).

open.name: sustainable_tree_has_sustainable_predecessor_closer_to_path
open.informal: Every sustainable tree X on Fin n (n ≥ 1) that is not isomorphic to the path graph pathGraph n has a sustainable generalized-tree-shift predecessor Y whose adjacency spectral radius is strictly smaller: there are vertices u ≠ v and a path p from u to v in Y through degree-2 interior vertices with X = gts_graph Y u v p.penultimate.
open.statement:
theorem sustainable_tree_has_sustainable_predecessor_closer_to_path
    (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) (X : SimpleGraph (Fin n))
    (hX : is_sustainable_tree X)
    (hXp : ¬ Nonempty (X ≃g SimpleGraph.pathGraph n)) :
    ∃ Y : SimpleGraph (Fin n),
      is_sustainable_tree Y ∧ is_generalized_tree_shift Y X ∧
      adjacency_spectral_radius Y < adjacency_spectral_radius X

open.name: temporal_path_snapshots_explore_n_log_n
open.informal: Open problem (arXiv:2610.06228, Sec. 7): temporal graphs whose snapshots are all spanning paths can always be explored in O(n log n) steps; i.e. there is a constant C such that every such temporal graph on n ≥ 2 vertices can be explored from any start vertex within C·n·log n time steps. (A disproof shows that the exploration time can exceed Θ(n log n).)
open.statement:
theorem temporal_path_snapshots_explore_n_log_n :
    ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ n : ℕ, 2 ≤ n → ∀ G : ℕ → SimpleGraph (Fin n), (∀ t, is_spanning_path_graph (G t)) →
      ∀ s : Fin n, ∃ (w : ℕ → Fin n) (T : ℕ), w 0 = s ∧ is_temporal_walk G w ∧
        temporal_walk_explores_by w T ∧ (T : ℝ) ≤ C * n * Real.log n
open.citation: open question of arXiv:2610.06228 (Hiding a Vertex from the Temporal Explorer), Sec. 7 ('The role of the hub'): the best known lower bound for path snapshots is Ω(n log n) and it is unknown whether it can be improved; the general upper bound is O(n²)

open.name: tournament_dijoin_inversion_number_symm
open.informal: Conjecture (arXiv:2610.13798, Conjecture 4.1): for all finite tournaments D₁, D₂, inv(D₁ → D₂) = inv(D₂ → D₁).
open.statement:
theorem tournament_dijoin_inversion_number_symm :
    ∀ (V W : Type) [Fintype V] [Fintype W] (D₁ : Digraph V) (D₂ : Digraph W),
      digraph_is_tournament D₁ → digraph_is_tournament D₂ →
      digraph_inversion_number (digraph_dijoin D₁ D₂) =
        digraph_inversion_number (digraph_dijoin D₂ D₁)
open.citation: arXiv:2610.13798 (On the failure of additivity of inversion numbers for dijoins), Conjecture 4.1 (posed earlier by other authors as their Conjecture 1.11). The paper shows inv(D₁ → D₂) can be far below inv(D₁) + inv(D₂), notes |inv(D₁ → D₂) − inv(D₂ → D₁)| ≤ 2, and suspects asymmetry for large tournaments.

open.name: tournament_inversion_number_le_min_rank_add_one
open.informal: For a finite tournament D: inv(D) ≤ tmr(D) + 1.
open.statement:
theorem tournament_inversion_number_le_min_rank_add_one (V : Type) [Fintype V] (D : Digraph V)
    (h : digraph_is_tournament D) :
    digraph_inversion_number D ≤ tournament_min_rank D + 1
open.citation: arXiv:2610.13798 (On the failure of additivity of inversion numbers for dijoins), inequality (1.2), quoting an earlier paper.

open.name: tuza_iff_tuza_of_edge_count_ge
open.informal: Tuza's conjecture holds for all finite graphs if and only if, for every c ≥ 0, it holds for all graphs on n ≥ n₀(c) vertices with at least n²/4 − cn edges.
open.statement:
theorem tuza_iff_tuza_of_edge_count_ge :
    (∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)),
      simple_graph_triangle_cover_number G ≤ 2 * simple_graph_triangle_packing_number G) ↔
    ∀ c : ℝ, 0 ≤ c → ∃ n₀ : ℕ, ∀ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj],
      n₀ ≤ n → (n : ℝ) ^ 2 / 4 - c * n ≤ G.edgeFinset.card →
        simple_graph_triangle_cover_number G ≤ 2 * simple_graph_triangle_packing_number G
open.citation: arXiv:2610.15539 (Tuza's conjecture under an edge-count condition), Proposition 1.2.

open.name: wild_number_complete_graph_min_proper_coloring_eq
open.informal: Conjecture: for every n ≥ 3 and every minimum proper edge colouring ρ of K_n, wld_ρ(K_n) = ⌊4⌈n/2⌉/3⌋.
open.statement:
theorem wild_number_complete_graph_min_proper_coloring_eq (n k : ℕ) (hn : 3 ≤ n)
    (hk : (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)).lineGraph.chromaticNumber = k)
    (c : (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)).lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)) :
    simple_graph_wild_number (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) c = 4 * ((n + 1) / 2) / 3
open.citation: arXiv:2610.22142 (Wild number for spanning trees in complete and complete bipartite graphs), Conjecture in Sec. 6 (verified there by computer for 3 ≤ n ≤ 12, Theorem 3.5; the lower bound is Theorem 3.4).

open.name: linear_code_supports_rate_unit_edge
open.informal: Non-vacuity of LinearCodeSupportsRate: on the two-vertex graph with a single unit-capacity edge, with the single session 0 -> 1, a deterministic causal binary linear network code with one transmission slot and one message symbol (T = 1, L = 1, M = 1) supports rate 1.
open.statement:
theorem linear_code_supports_rate_unit_edge :
  ∃ (net : CapacitatedNetwork (Fin 2)) (sess : UnicastSessions (Fin 2) (Fin 1)),
    net.cap s((0 : Fin 2), (1 : Fin 2)) = 1 ∧
    sess.src (0 : Fin 1) = (0 : Fin 2) ∧ sess.tgt (0 : Fin 1) = (1 : Fin 2) ∧
    LinearCodeSupportsRate (ZMod 2) net sess 1

open.name: mutual_power_divergence_information_subadditive_of_two_thirds_le
open.informal: Conjecture: for every β ∈ [2/3, 1), the mutual f_β-information (power divergence) is subadditive under Y ← X → Z: Ĩ_{f_β}(X; YZ) ≤ Ĩ_{f_β}(X; Y) + Ĩ_{f_β}(X; Z). (It fails at β = 1/4 and β = 1/2.)
open.statement:
theorem mutual_power_divergence_information_subadditive_of_two_thirds_le {X Y Z : Type*}
    [Fintype X] [Fintype Y] [Fintype Z] (β : ℝ) (hβ0 : 2 / 3 ≤ β) (hβ1 : β < 1) (pX : X → ℝ)
    (PY : X → Y → ℝ) (PZ : X → Z → ℝ) (hpX : ∀ x, 0 ≤ pX x) (hpX1 : ∑ x, pX x = 1)
    (hPY : ∀ x y, 0 ≤ PY x y) (hPY1 : ∀ x, ∑ y, PY x y = 1)
    (hPZ : ∀ x z, 0 ≤ PZ x z) (hPZ1 : ∀ x, ∑ z, PZ x z = 1) :
    mutual_f_information (power_divergence_generator β)
        (fun x (yz : Y × Z) => pX x * PY x yz.1 * PZ x yz.2) ≤
      mutual_f_information (power_divergence_generator β) (fun x y => pX x * PY x y) +
        mutual_f_information (power_divergence_generator β) (fun x z => pX x * PZ x z)
open.citation: arXiv:2610.21231 (On the subadditivity of mutual f-information), Theorem 1 (a sufficient differential condition for subadditivity, met by the Kullback–Leibler generator but not by power divergences) and the question after it; refutations at β = 1/4 and 1/2 are in the knowledge base.

open.name: single_slot_binary_linear_coding_advantage
open.informal: Normal form of OP-90: there exist a finite vertex set, a finite session type, a capacitated network, unicast sessions and a deterministic causal binary linear code on them with exactly one transmission slot (T = 1) whose rate, the number L of message symbols per session, is strictly greater than every rate supported by fractional multicommodity flow on the same instance. This is the residual open content after normalisation, not a step that is easier than the target: read a T-slot code on capacities c as a one-slot code on capacities T*c (T is the only place the slot count occurs, in cap_le, and flow feasibility is homogeneous of degree one in (f, r, c)), so every T-slot witness yields a one-slot witness, and conversely the target follows from this statement in one line with r := (code.L : ℝ).
open.statement:
theorem single_slot_binary_linear_coding_advantage :
  ∃ (V : Type) (_ : Fintype V) (_ : DecidableEq V)
    (K : Type) (_ : Fintype K) (_ : DecidableEq K)
    (net : CapacitatedNetwork V) (sess : UnicastSessions V K)
    (code : CausalLinearNetworkCode V K (ZMod 2) net sess),
    code.T = 1 ∧
    ∀ r_flow, FlowSupportsRate net sess r_flow → r_flow < (code.L : ℝ)

open.name: undirected_binary_linear_unicast_advantage
open.informal: Open Problem OP-90: there exist a finite vertex type V with decidable equality, a finite session type K with decidable equality, a capacitated network net on V, unicast sessions sess on V indexed by K, and a rate r ∈ ℝ such that LinearCodeSupportsRate (ZMod 2) net sess r holds, and for every r_flow such that FlowSupportsRate net sess r_flow holds, r_flow < r.
open.statement:
theorem undirected_binary_linear_unicast_advantage :
  ∃ (V : Type) (_ : Fintype V) (_ : DecidableEq V)
    (K : Type) (_ : Fintype K) (_ : DecidableEq K)
    (net : CapacitatedNetwork V) (sess : UnicastSessions V K) (r : ℝ),
    LinearCodeSupportsRate (ZMod 2) net sess r ∧
    ∀ r_flow, FlowSupportsRate net sess r_flow → r_flow < r

open.name: op182_deferred_to_deadline_beyond_half_against_stopping
open.informal: Refutation of Open Problem OP-182 against the deferred-until-stopping benchmark: there does not exist any constant `c > 1/2` such that for every Pandora's problem instance with deadlines `inst : PandoraDeadlineInstance`, there exists a valid adaptive policy `π` satisfying `IsValidPolicy inst π` whose expected utility under deferred-to-deadline commitment `expectedUtilityDTD inst π` is at least `c * optDUS inst`.
open.statement:
theorem op182_deferred_to_deadline_beyond_half_against_stopping :
    ¬ (∃ c > (1 / 2 : ℝ), ∀ inst : PandoraDeadlineInstance,
        ∃ π : AdaptivePolicy inst.n, IsValidPolicy inst π ∧
          c * optDUS inst ≤ expectedUtilityDTD inst π)

open.name: two_box_counterexample_family
open.informal: For any integer `M > 1`, there exists a 2-box Pandora deadline instance such that `2 - 1 / M ≤ optDUS inst` and every valid policy `π` achieves `expectedUtilityDTD inst π ≤ 1`.
open.statement:
theorem two_box_counterexample_family (M : ℕ) (hM : 1 < M) :
    ∃ inst : PandoraDeadlineInstance,
      2 - (1 : ℝ) / M ≤ optDUS inst ∧
      ∀ π : AdaptivePolicy inst.n, IsValidPolicy inst π → expectedUtilityDTD inst π ≤ 1

open.name: resolution_fpt_incidence_treewidth
open.informal: Open problem (arXiv:2610.02047, abstract and Sec. 8): every unsatisfiable CNF formula has an FPT-sized resolution refutation parameterized by incidence treewidth; that is, there are a computable g : N -> N and a constant c >= 1 such that every unsatisfiable CNF formula F with n variables and m clauses has a resolution refutation (initial clauses, weakening, resolution) of length at most g(tw*(F)) * (n + m)^c.
open.statement: theorem resolution_fpt_incidence_treewidth : ∃ g : ℕ → ℕ, Computable g ∧ ∃ c : ℕ, 1 ≤ c ∧ ∀ F : Finset (Finset (CnfLit ℕ)), ¬ CnfSatisfiable (F.toList.map Finset.toList) → ∃ π, is_resolution_refutation F π ∧ π.length ≤ g (cnf_incidence_treewidth F) * ((cnf_vars F).card + F.card) ^ c
open.citation: the open problem of arXiv:2610.02047, abstract and Sec. 8 (FPT-sized resolution refutations parameterized by incidence treewidth), stated as posed

open.name: ccz_layer_t_count_below_6m_plus_1_with_hadamards
open.informal: Open problem (arXiv:2610.01024, abstract and Sec. 1): in general Clifford+T circuits, with Hadamards anywhere and any number of clean ancillas, some layer of m >= 2 disjoint CCZ gates can be implemented with strictly fewer than 6m + 1 T gates (the exact count 6m + 1 is proved only for Hadamard-free circuits).
open.statement: theorem ccz_layer_t_count_below_6m_plus_1_with_hadamards : ∃ m : ℕ, 2 ≤ m ∧ ∃ (a : ℕ) (gs : List (CliffordTGate (3 * m + a))), implements_ccz_layer m a gs ∧ clifford_t_circuit_t_count gs < 6 * m + 1
open.citation: the open problem of arXiv:2610.01024, abstract and Sec. 1 (fewer than 6m + 1 T gates with Hadamards and ancillas), stated as posed; related: its Corollary 83

open.name: open_problem_line_cubic_t_count
open.informal: For every integer n ≥ 5, there exists a parity representation of the line cubic syndrome of cardinality 2n + 1.
open.statement: theorem open_problem_line_cubic_t_count (n : ℕ) (hn : 5 ≤ n) : ∃ S : Finset (Finset (Fin n)), is_parity_repr S (line_syndrome n) ∧ S.card = 2 * n + 1

literature.title: Existence of a 22-multiplication algorithm for 3x3 matrix multiplication over ℤ
literature.statement: Does there exist an algorithm for 3x3 matrix multiplication with integer constants that can be applied recursively (or equivalently, a bilinear decomposition of the 3x3 matrix multiplication tensor over ℤ) using 22 multiplications, or is 23 multiplications the minimum?
literature.source_title: Lower Bound of 22 for 3x3 Matrix Multiplication over the Integers
literature.rationale: The authors prove a lower bound of 22 multiplications for any recursive 3x3 algorithm with integer constants, improving the previous bound of 21. Laderman's 1976 algorithm provides an upper bound of 23. Whether 22 is achievable over the integers remains unresolved.

literature.title: Tensor rank of 3x3 matrix multiplication over F2
literature.statement: Is the tensor rank of 3x3 matrix multiplication over the finite field F2 equal to 22 or 23? That is, does there exist a set of 22 triad products whose F2-linear combinations compute the product of two arbitrary 3x3 matrices over F2, or is the rank at least 23?
literature.source_title: Lower Bound of 22 for 3x3 Matrix Multiplication over the Integers
literature.rationale: The paper proves in Lean that the tensor rank of 3x3 matrix multiplication over F2 is at least 22 (class 495 in Wang's table), improving on the lower bound of 21 from Wang (2026) and Yang et al. (2026). Laderman's 1976 decomposition yields an upper bound of 23 over F2. Thus the exact rank over F2 is either 22 or 23, leaving a gap of exactly one.

literature.title: T-count of parallel CCZ gates in general Clifford+T with Hadamards
literature.statement: Let m ≥ 2 be an integer, and let U_m = ⨂_{j=1}^m CCZ_{3j-2, 3j-1, 3j} be the unitary operator on 3m qubits that acts as the three-qubit Controlled-Controlled-Z gate CCZ = diag(1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, -1) on each disjoint triplet of qubits (3j-2, 3j-1, 3j). In a general Clifford+T quantum circuit with an arbitrary number a ≥ 0 of clean ancilla qubits (initialized and returned to |0⟩), where gates may be arbitrary single-qubit Hadamards H, phase gates S = diag(1, i), CNOT gates, and T = diag(1, e^{iπ/4}) gates: can U_m be implemented using strictly fewer than 6m + 1 gates of type T?
literature.source_title: Exact $T$-counts of Toffoli layers from an isotropy bound
literature.rationale: The paper proves that every Hadamard-free Clifford+T circuit with clean ancillas implementing m disjoint CCZ gates requires at least 6m+1 T gates, which matches the Campbell-Howard construction. However, general Clifford+T circuits may place Hadamard gates freely between T gates. For m = 1, it is known that CCZ requires 7 T gates even with Hadamards, but for m ≥ 2 it is unknown whether intermediate Hadamard gates can reduce the T-count below 6m+1.

literature.title: Exact T-count of the line cubic phase gate family
literature.statement: For an integer n ≥ 5, let f_n : (ZMod 2)^n → ZMod 2 be the cubic form f_n(x_1, ..., x_n) = ∑_{i=1}^{n-2} x_i x_{i+1} x_{i+2}, and let U_{f_n} be the diagonal n-qubit gate acting by |x⟩ ↦ (-1)^{f_n(x)} |x⟩. Let δ(U_{f_n}) denote the minimum number of T gates required to implement U_{f_n} in a Hadamard-free {CNOT, T} circuit with diagonal Clifford gates free. By Proposition 65, δ(U_{f_n}) ≥ 2n + 1 for all n ≥ 5, with equality δ(U_{f_n}) = 2n + 1 known to hold for 5 ≤ n ≤ 12. Does δ(U_{f_n}) = 2n + 1 hold for all n ≥ 5?
literature.source_title: Exact $T$-counts of Toffoli layers from an isotropy bound

literature.title: Exact T-count of the GF(8) multiplication oracle
literature.statement: Let U_3 be the reversible multiplication oracle for the finite field GF(8) = GF(2^3) acting on 9 qubits by |a, b, c⟩ ↦ |a, b, c ⊕ (a · b)⟩ for a, b, c ∈ GF(8). Under Clifford equivalence to a diagonal level-three gate, its T-count δ(U_3) in Hadamard-free {CNOT, T} circuits with clean ancillas is known to satisfy 20 ≤ δ(U_3) ≤ 23, where 20 is the slice-rank lower bound (Proposition 59) and 23 is achieved by known compiled circuits. What is the exact T-count δ(U_3) of the GF(8) oracle? Specifically, is it 20, 23, or an intermediate value (21 or 22)?
literature.source_title: Exact $T$-counts of Toffoli layers from an isotropy bound

literature.title: FPT-sized resolution refutations parameterized by incidence treewidth
literature.statement: Does every unsatisfiable CNF formula have an FPT-sized resolution refutation parameterized by its incidence treewidth? Precisely: do there exist a computable function $g: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a constant $c \ge 1$ such that for every unsatisfiable CNF formula $F$ with $n$ variables and $m$ clauses, there exists a resolution refutation of $F$ of length at most $g(\mathrm{tw}^*(F)) (n+m)^c$? Here, a CNF formula $F$ is a finite set of clauses over a finite set of Boolean variables $V$, where each clause is a finite disjunction of literals (variables or their negations); the incidence graph $G^*(F)$ is the bipartite graph with vertex set $V \cup F$ and edges $\{x, C\}$ for every variable $x \in \mathrm{var}(C)$; $\mathrm{tw}^*(F)$ is the treewidth of $G^*(F)$; and a resolution refutation is a sequence of clauses ending in $\bot$ derived by weakening and resolution.
literature.source_title: Short Resolution Refutations for CNFs with Bounded Weighted Incidence Treewidth
literature.rationale: Central open question in parameterized proof complexity, explicitly highlighted in the paper's abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

literature.title: EFX existence for four or more agents with additive goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. An allocation is an ordered partition $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$ (every good is allocated; bundles may be empty). The allocation is EFX (envy-free up to any good) if for all agents $i\ne j$ and every good $g\in A_j$ we have $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$. Question: for every $n\ge 4$, every $m$ and every additive valuation profile, does an EFX allocation exist? (Some papers quantify only over $g$ with $v_i(g)>0$; for strictly positive values the two versions coincide, and both are open. The smallest open case is $n=4$.)
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.location: Sec. 4.1, Open Problem 2 (EFX itself first proposed in 'The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare', ACM TEAC 2019, DOI:10.1145/3355902, which left existence open)
literature.rationale: Widely called the central open problem of discrete fair division. Known: $n=2$ (cut-and-choose, arXiv:1707.04769); $n=3$ with additive valuations ('EFX Exists for Three Agents', arXiv:2002.05119), extended to three agents when at least one valuation is additive/MMS-feasible (arXiv:2205.07638); EFX with at most one unallocated good for $n=4$ (arXiv:2102.10654); EFX with at most $n-2$ unallocated goods in general (arXiv:2102.10654, arXiv:2107.09901); complete EFX when $m\le n+3$ and, for $n=4$, when $m\le 9$ (arXiv:2608.08590, computer-assisted); EFX for up to three valuation types ('EFX Exists for Three Types of Agents', EC 2025); EF2X for four agents (arXiv:2412.00254); EFX on multigraph instances (arXiv:2606.18665). On the negative side, EFX fails for three agents with monotone submodular valuations (arXiv:2604.18216, arXiv:2605.06451) and for $n\ge 4$ additive chores (arXiv:2606.08872), but no additive-goods counterexample is known.

literature.title: EFX for three agents with additive chores
literature.statement: There are $3$ agents and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible chores. Agent $i$ has an additive cost function $c_i(S)=\sum_{e\in S}c_i(e)$ with $c_i(e)\ge 0$. An allocation is a partition $A=(A_1,A_2,A_3)$ of $M$ (all chores assigned). It is EFX for chores if for all agents $i\ne j$ and every chore $e\in A_i$, $c_i(A_i\setminus\{e\})\le c_i(A_j)$. Question: does every such 3-agent instance admit an EFX allocation? (Variant quantifying only over $e$ with $c_i(e)>0$ is equally open; with strictly positive costs they coincide.)
literature.source_title: EFX for Additive Chores: Nonexistence, Pareto Incompatibility, and Bi-Valued Existence
literature.location: Sec. 1 (introduction) and Sec. 6 (open problems); the n=3 gap is also the explicit frontier in arXiv:2609.10585
literature.rationale: After the 2026 counterexample for every $n\ge 4$ (tri-valued costs, two agent types, three chore types; arXiv:2606.08872), three agents is the only remaining number of agents for which EFX existence under additive costs is undecided (two agents is easy by cut-and-choose). Known for $n=3$: all instances with $m\le 8$ chores (arXiv:2609.10585, SMT-verified); personalized bi-valued instances; EFX together with fractional Pareto optimality for bi-valued costs; instances with $m\le 2n$; two chore types. Approximate EFX results exist (e.g. arXiv:2410.18655). A small-$n$ question with a finite search frontier ($m=9$ next), so it is a natural target for computer-assisted search and Lean-checked certificates.

literature.title: Best universal approximation ratio for maximin share with additive goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. An allocation is an ordered partition $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$ (every good is allocated; bundles may be empty). The maximin share of agent $i$ is $\mu_i=\max_{(P_1,\dots,P_n)}\min_k v_i(P_k)$, the maximum over all partitions of $M$ into $n$ bundles. For $\alpha\in(0,1]$ an allocation is $\alpha$-MMS if $v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,\mu_i$ for every $i$. Let $\alpha^*$ be the supremum of $\alpha$ such that every instance (any $n$, $m$, additive $v$) admits an $\alpha$-MMS allocation. Question: determine $\alpha^*$; currently $7/9\le\alpha^*\le 20/21$.
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.rationale: Exact MMS allocations need not exist for $n\ge 3$, so the right constant is a central question. Lower bounds: $3/4+3/3836$ (arXiv:2307.07304), $10/13$ (arXiv:2510.10423), and $7/9$ with an FPTAS for $7/9-\varepsilon$ (arXiv:2511.13056). Upper bounds: $39/40$ for three agents (arXiv:2104.04977), improved to $20/21$ with four agents and eleven goods, together with an asymptotic bound $1-\Omega((\log n)^{-2})$ (arXiv:2609.15085). The gap $[0.778, 0.952]$ remains wide.

literature.title: Best universal approximation ratio for maximin share with additive chores
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents and a finite set $M$ of indivisible chores; agent $i$ has an additive cost $c_i(S)=\sum_{e\in S}c_i(e)$ with $c_i(e)\ge 0$. An allocation partitions $M$ into $(A_1,\dots,A_n)$. The maximin share (for chores) is $\mu_i=\min_{(P_1,\dots,P_n)}\max_k c_i(P_k)$ over all partitions of $M$ into $n$ bundles. For $\beta\ge 1$ an allocation is $\beta$-MMS if $c_i(A_i)\le\beta\,\mu_i$ for all $i$. Let $\beta^*$ be the infimum of $\beta$ such that every instance admits a $\beta$-MMS allocation. Question: determine $\beta^*$; currently $31/30\le\beta^*\le 13/11$.
literature.source_title: Approximation Algorithms for Max-Min Share Allocations of Indivisible Chores and Goods
literature.rationale: The chores counterpart of OP-9, introduced in arXiv:1604.01435 (which showed exact MMS can fail for chores and gave a 2-approximation). Existence bound $13/11$ through a reduction to the MultiFit job-scheduling algorithm (arXiv:2302.04581), with better bounds for small $n$ ($15/13$ for $n=3$ there; $19/18$ for three agents in arXiv:2205.05363). Impossibility $44/43$ with three agents (arXiv:2104.04977), improved to $31/30$ with four agents and eleven chores, plus asymptotic $1+\Omega((\log n)^{-2})$ (arXiv:2609.15085).

literature.title: Maximin share approximation for three agents with additive goods
literature.statement: Same model as the general MMS problem (see OP-9) with exactly $n=3$ agents: finite goods set $M$, additive $v_i\ge 0$, $\mu_i=\max$ over partitions of $M$ into 3 bundles of the minimum bundle value, and an allocation is $\alpha$-MMS if $v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\mu_i$ for $i=1,2,3$. Let $\alpha_3^*$ be the largest $\alpha$ such that every 3-agent instance admits an $\alpha$-MMS allocation. Question: determine $\alpha_3^*$; currently $11/12\le\alpha_3^*\le 39/40$.
literature.source_title: Improved maximin fair allocation of indivisible items to three agents
literature.rationale: The smallest case where exact MMS can fail. The $11/12$ guarantee (arXiv:2205.05363) is shown best possible for a restricted kind of allocation (one prespecified agent gets her full proportional share), so improving it needs new ideas. The $39/40$ example (three agents, nine goods; arXiv:2104.04977) is proven to be the worst possible among instances with fewer than six more items than agents, so any better impossibility needs at least ten goods. With three agents the problem is small enough for computer-assisted search on the impossibility side.

literature.title: Polynomial-time computation of EF1 and Pareto-optimal allocations of goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. An allocation is an ordered partition $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$ (every good is allocated; bundles may be empty). Values are given as nonnegative integers (or rationals) in binary. An allocation is EF1 if for all $i\ne j$ with $A_j\ne\emptyset$ there is $g\in A_j$ with $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$, and Pareto optimal (PO) if no allocation $B$ has $v_i(B_i)\ge v_i(A_i)$ for all $i$ with strict inequality for some $i$. An EF1+PO allocation always exists (e.g. a maximum Nash welfare allocation). Question: is there an algorithm that outputs an EF1+PO allocation in time polynomial in $n$, $m$ and the bit length of the values?
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.rationale: Existence follows from maximum Nash welfare ('The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare'), but computing that allocation is APX-hard. A market-based pseudo-polynomial algorithm finds EF1+PO (arXiv:1707.04731); polynomial time is known for a fixed number of agents (arXiv:2411.01810), for binary and other few-valued instances, and for EF1+fPO under extra structure. For chores, EF1+PO existence was settled in 2025 (arXiv:2507.09544), but only with polynomial time for constant $n$. A general polynomial algorithm, or evidence of hardness (e.g. PLS/PPAD), is open.

literature.title: EF1 and Pareto optimality for mixed goods and chores
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents and a finite set $M$ of indivisible items. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{o\in S}v_i(o)$ with $v_i(o)\in\mathbb{R}$ of arbitrary sign (an item may be a good for one agent and a chore for another). An allocation is a partition $(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$. It is EF1 if for all $i\ne j$, either $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j)$ or there is an item $o\in A_i\cup A_j$ with $v_i(A_i\setminus\{o\})\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{o\})$. It is Pareto optimal if no allocation $B$ has $v_i(B_i)\ge v_i(A_i)$ for all $i$ with strict inequality for some $i$. Question: does every such instance (for every $n\ge 3$) admit an allocation that is both EF1 and Pareto optimal?
literature.source_title: Fair allocation of combinations of indivisible goods and chores
literature.rationale: For goods, maximum Nash welfare gives EF1+PO; for chores, existence was proven only in 2025 by a fixed-point argument (arXiv:2507.09544). For mixed manna, EF1 alone is easy (a double round-robin) and EF1+PO is known for two agents (arXiv:1807.10684), but the general case is open, even for three agents. Partial progress: PO with introspective EF1 (arXiv:2509.18673) and PO with envy-freeness up to $n-1$ reallocations (arXiv:2507.03946). A positive answer would unify the goods and chores theories.

literature.title: Query complexity of envy-free cake cutting
literature.statement: The cake is $[0,1]$. Each of $n$ agents has a valuation $v_i$: a nonatomic probability measure on $[0,1]$ (additive, $v_i([0,1])=1$, single points have measure 0). In the Robertson–Webb query model a protocol may ask $\mathrm{Eval}_i(x,y)=v_i([x,y])$ and $\mathrm{Cut}_i(x,\alpha)=$ some $y$ with $v_i([x,y])=\alpha$. It must output an allocation: disjoint pieces $A_1,\dots,A_n$, each a finite union of intervals, covering $[0,1]$, that is envy-free ($v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j)$ for all $i,j$). Let $T(n)$ be the minimum, over protocols, of the worst-case number of queries. Question: is $T(n)$ bounded by a polynomial in $n$? More generally, determine the growth of $T(n)$.
literature.source_title: A Discrete and Bounded Envy-Free Cake Cutting Protocol for Any Number of Agents
literature.rationale: Bounded protocols were found only in 2015-16: four agents (arXiv:1508.05143, improved to about 171 queries in arXiv:1807.00317) and any $n$ with a tower of exponentials (arXiv:1604.03655). A later sharper analysis gave $n^{O(n^2)}$, and a September 2026 preprint claims $n^{O(1)}2^n$ (arXiv:2609.05191; not yet peer-reviewed). The only lower bound is $\Omega(n^2)$ ('Thou Shalt Covet Thy Neighbor's Cake'). Even for $n=4$ the exact query complexity is unknown. With connected pieces, exact envy-freeness cannot be reached by any finite protocol, and the connected approximate version is a separate open question (see OP-18).

literature.title: Best approximation factor for EFX with additive goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. An allocation is an ordered partition $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$ (every good is allocated; bundles may be empty). For $\alpha\in(0,1]$ an allocation is $\alpha$-EFX if for all $i\ne j$ and all $g\in A_j$, $v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$. Let $\alpha^*$ be the supremum of $\alpha$ such that every instance (any $n$, $m$) admits an $\alpha$-EFX allocation. Currently $\varphi-1=(\sqrt5-1)/2\approx0.618\le\alpha^*\le 1$. Question: determine $\alpha^*$; in particular, does a $2/3$-EFX allocation (or any $\alpha>\varphi-1$) always exist for every $n$?
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.rationale: Envy-cycle elimination gives $1/2$-EFX, and the golden-ratio bound $\varphi-1$ comes from combining round-robin with envy-cycle elimination ('Multiple Birds with One Stone: Beating 1/2 for EFX and GMMS via Envy Cycle Elimination', arXiv:1909.07650). $2/3$-EFX is known for at most seven agents, for valuations with at most three distinct values, and for multigraph instances (arXiv:2406.12413), and $(1-\varepsilon)$-EFX holds if a sublinear number of goods may stay unallocated (arXiv:2205.07638). If OP-7 were refuted, this question would become the main open problem about EFX.

literature.title: EFX together with Pareto optimality for positive additive goods
literature.statement: There are $n\ge 3$ agents and a finite set $M$ of goods; agent $i$ has an additive valuation with strictly positive item values $v_i(g)>0$. An allocation $(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ partitions $M$. It is EFX if $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$ for all $i\ne j$ and $g\in A_j$, and Pareto optimal if no allocation $B$ has $v_i(B_i)\ge v_i(A_i)$ for all $i$ with strict inequality for some $i$. Question: does every such instance admit an allocation that is simultaneously EFX and Pareto optimal? (The case $n=3$, where EFX alone is known to exist, is already open.)
literature.source_title: Almost Envy-Freeness with General Valuations
literature.rationale: With zero values EFX and PO can be incompatible even for two agents (arXiv:1707.04769), so strict positivity is the natural assumption; with it, EFX+PO holds for two agents via leximin. Known: bi-valued instances (EFX with fractional PO); two types of goods (arXiv:2601.03438). For chores the analog fails for every $n\ge 4$ even with positive bi-valued costs (arXiv:2606.08872), which raises the question of whether goods behave differently. A counterexample for $n=3$ would be a finite object, which makes this attractive for search plus Lean verification.

literature.title: Exact EFX with a sublinear number of unallocated goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. A partial allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles $X_1,\dots,X_n\subseteq M$; the unallocated goods form $P=M\setminus\bigcup_i X_i$. $X$ is EFX if $v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(X_j\setminus\{g\})$ for all $i\ne j$, $g\in X_j$, and no agent envies the pool if $v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(P)$ for all $i$. It is known that some EFX partial allocation with no envy toward the pool always has $|P|\le n-2$ (for $n\ge 2$). Question: is there a function $f(n)=o(n)$ such that every additive instance admits an EFX partial allocation with $|P|\le f(n)$ and no agent envying the pool?
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.rationale: EFX with charity was introduced in arXiv:1902.04319, with the bound of $n-1$ unallocated goods in arXiv:1907.04596, improved to $n-2$ (arXiv:2102.10654; arXiv:2107.09901 for general monotone valuations). Through the rainbow-cycle-number connection, $(1-\varepsilon)$-EFX holds with sublinearly many unallocated goods ($\tilde O((n/\varepsilon)^{1/2})$, arXiv:2205.07638), but for exact EFX nothing sublinear is known. A positive answer to OP-7 would give $f\equiv0$, so this is a weaker stepping stone toward OP-7.

literature.title: Connected approximately envy-free cake cutting for five monotone agents
literature.statement: The cake is $[0,1]$. Each of $n=5$ agents has a valuation $v_i$ assigning a value in $[0,1]$ to every interval $I\subseteq[0,1]$. It is monotone ($I\subseteq J\Rightarrow v_i(I)\le v_i(J)$), Lipschitz-continuous in the endpoints, and accessible only through value queries $v_i([a,b])$. A connected allocation is given by cut points $0\le x_1\le\dots\le x_4\le 1$, which form 5 consecutive intervals, together with a bijection assigning them to agents. It is $\varepsilon$-envy-free if $v_i(I_{\sigma(i)})\ge v_i(I_{\sigma(j)})-\varepsilon$ for all $i,j$. Such allocations always exist. Question: can one be found with $\mathrm{poly}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ value queries, or is $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ queries necessary?
literature.source_title: Envy-Free Cake-Cutting for Four Agents
literature.rationale: For monotone valuations an efficient algorithm ($\mathrm{poly}(\log 1/\varepsilon)$ queries) was known for three agents ('Algorithmic Solutions for Envy-Free Cake Cutting', Operations Research 2012, which posed four or more agents as open), and arXiv:2311.02075 solved four agents. Without monotonicity the problem becomes PPAD-hard with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ query lower bounds for four agents (arXiv:2311.02075), and in 2026 also for three agents (arXiv:2606.13980). Five monotone agents is the next frontier, and it decides whether monotonicity keeps the problem tractable for every $n$.

literature.title: Condorcet dimension of elections: do 3 candidates always suffice?
literature.statement: Let $N$ be a finite nonempty set of $n$ voters and $C$ a finite set of candidates; each voter $v$ has a strict linear order $\succ_v$ on $C$. A set $S \subseteq C$ is a Condorcet winning set if for every candidate $a \in C \setminus S$, strictly fewer than $n/2$ voters rank $a$ above every member of $S$ (equivalently, a strict majority of voters prefers some member of $S$ to $a$). The Condorcet dimension of the election is the minimum size of a Condorcet winning set. Question: is the Condorcet dimension of every election at most 3? (Weaker open form: at most 4.) It is known that every election has dimension at most 5, and that there exist elections of dimension exactly 3.
literature.source_title: Condorcet winning sets
literature.rationale: The concept was introduced in the paper 'Condorcet winning sets', which exhibited elections needing 3 candidates and conjectured unbounded dimension. 'Six Candidates Suffice to Win a Voter Majority' (arXiv:2411.03390) gave the first constant bound (6) via the minimax theorem and maximal lotteries; 'A few good choices' (arXiv:2506.22133) improved it to 5 (exposition: arXiv:2606.14666). 'Is Four Enough? Automated Reasoning Approaches and Dual Bounds for Condorcet Dimensions of Elections' (arXiv:2604.19851) reports extensive SAT/computational search finding no election of dimension > 3 and states the gap 3 <= k <= 5 as open. Special cases: dimension <= 3 for l1 and l_inf metric elections (arXiv:2410.09201) and for planar Euclidean metric elections (arXiv:2608.27653). Closing the gap is a central question in committee selection and connects to approximately dominating sets (arXiv:2504.20372, arXiv:2608.06872).

literature.title: Optimal metric distortion of randomized ordinal voting rules
literature.statement: Voters $V$ ($|V|=n$) and candidates $C$ ($|C|=m$) lie in a common (pseudo)metric space $d$. Each voter reports a strict ranking of $C$ consistent with $d$ (if $d(v,a)<d(v,b)$ then $v$ ranks $a$ above $b$). A randomized ordinal rule $f$ maps each ranking profile $\sigma$ to a probability distribution over $C$. Social cost: $SC_d(c)=\sum_{v\in V} d(v,c)$. The distortion of $f$ is $\sup_{n,m,\sigma}\ \sup_{d \text{ consistent with } \sigma} \mathbb{E}_{c\sim f(\sigma)}[SC_d(c)] / \min_{c'} SC_d(c')$. Question: determine $\alpha^* = \inf_f \mathrm{dist}(f)$. Known: $2.1126 \le \alpha^* \le 2.13713$ (deterministic rules: optimal value is exactly 3).
literature.source_title: Metric Distortion Bounds for Randomized Social Choice
literature.rationale: A natural conjecture that randomized rules achieve distortion 2 was refuted by the lower bound approaching 2.1126 as the number of candidates grows ('Metric Distortion Bounds for Randomized Social Choice', arXiv:2111.03694). The first constant separation from 3 was 2.753 ('Breaking the Metric Voting Distortion Barrier', arXiv:2306.17838). In Aug-Sep 2026 the upper bound dropped rapidly: 5/2 ('An improved bound for the randomized metric distortion problem', arXiv:2608.17863), 2.1441 ('Improving Randomized Metric Distortion to 2.1441', arXiv:2608.29308), and 2.13713 ('Stable Voting Rules on the Edge of Optimal Metric Distortion', arXiv:2609.08259), within 0.025 of the lower bound. The exact optimum, and whether the lower-bound construction is tight, remain open. The m=3 case is resolved exactly in arXiv:2111.03694.

literature.title: Maximum size of a Condorcet domain
literature.statement: A Condorcet domain on the alternative set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a set $D$ of linear orders on $[n]$ such that for every finite profile of voters with an odd number of voters, each voter's order taken from $D$, the pairwise strict-majority relation is transitive. Equivalently, for every three alternatives $a,b,c$, the restrictions of the orders in $D$ to $\{a,b,c\}$ satisfy a never-condition: some $x\in\{a,b,c\}$ and some position $p\in\{1,2,3\}$ such that $x$ never appears at position $p$ in any restriction. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum $|D|$. Questions: (a) determine $f(9)$ (known $492 \le f(9)$); (b) determine $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(n)^{1/n}$ (known to be at least $2.198139$ and finite).
literature.source_title: Improved lower bounds for the maximum size of Condorcet domains
literature.location: Introduction (exact maximum only known for n <= 8)
literature.rationale: The maximum size of acyclic sets of linear orders is a classical question going back to the early 1990s literature on Condorcet domains. Exact values are known only up to n=8, where f(8)=224 with a unique extremal domain ('The Largest Condorcet Domains on 8 Alternatives', arXiv:2303.15002). Heuristic and supercomputer searches ('New Record-Breaking Condorcet Domains on 10 and 11 Alternatives', arXiv:2303.06524; arXiv:2601.07336) give f(9)>=492, f(10)>=1104, f(11)>=2452 and an asymptotic lower bound Omega(2.198139^n). An exponential upper bound c^n is known but with an implicit constant that gives no realistic value, so the growth rate is wide open. The n=9 case is a finite but very large search.

literature.title: Committee monotonicity versus EJR in approval-based committee voting
literature.statement: Let $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ be voters and $C$ a finite set of $m$ candidates; voter $i$ approves a set $A_i\subseteq C$. For a committee size $k$, a group $G\subseteq N$ is $\ell$-cohesive if $|G|\ge \ell n/k$ and $|\bigcap_{i\in G}A_i|\ge \ell$. A committee $W\subseteq C$ with $|W|=k$ satisfies Extended Justified Representation (EJR) if for every $\ell\ge 1$ and every $\ell$-cohesive group $G$ there is $i\in G$ with $|A_i\cap W|\ge \ell$. Question: does every approval profile admit an ordering $c_1,c_2,\dots,c_m$ of all candidates such that for every $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ the prefix $\{c_1,\dots,c_k\}$ satisfies EJR for committee size $k$? (Equivalently: does there exist a resolute committee-monotonic approval-based committee rule satisfying EJR?)
literature.source_title: Multi-Winner Voting with Approval Preferences
literature.location: Open problems chapter, Q2 (Committee monotonicity and proportionality)
literature.rationale: Committee monotonicity (W(k) ⊆ W(k+1)) is essential for ranking candidates/excellence lists. Sequential Phragmén is committee monotonic and satisfies the weaker PJR, while all known EJR rules (PAV, Method of Equal Shares) violate committee monotonicity. The survey states no impossibility is known and only partial answers exist: a positive answer is known for approval-based party-list elections ('Approval-Based Apportionment', arXiv:1911.08365). Because a resolute rule may be defined profile-by-profile, the question is exactly the per-profile chain-existence statement above, so a counterexample is a finite object that could be found by SAT search; a positive answer would require a new construction.

literature.title: Do 2-approximately stable committees always exist?
literature.statement: There are $n$ voters and a finite candidate set $C$ with unit weights; a committee is a subset $S\subseteq C$. Each voter $v$ has a complete transitive (weak) preference $\succeq_v$ over all subsets of $C$ that is monotone: $S_1\subseteq S_2 \Rightarrow S_2\succeq_v S_1$. Fix a size limit $K\ge1$. For $c\ge1$, a committee $S$ with $|S|\le K$ is $c$-approximately stable if for every committee $S'$ (of any size $K'=|S'|$), the number of voters who strictly prefer $S'$ to $S$ is strictly less than $c\,\frac{K'}{K}\,n$. ($c=1$ is the core.) Question: for every such instance, does a 2-approximately stable committee exist? It is known that $c$ cannot be below 2 in general, and that $c=32$ always suffices (16 when exactly stable lotteries exist).
literature.source_title: Approximately Stable Committee Selection
literature.location: Sec. 5 (Open Questions), last bullet; companion question: exactly stable lotteries (first bullet)
literature.rationale: Stability (core) is the strongest group-fairness notion for committee selection and covers participatory budgeting, facility location and ranking-based committee voting as special cases. Exactly stable committees can fail to exist (cyclic preferences), and Appendix A of arXiv:1910.14008 shows (2-eps)-stable committees may fail to exist even in the ranking setting with unit weights; the same paper proves an O(1) bound (32, improvable to 16 when exactly stable lotteries exist, e.g. ranking and approval settings via 'Group Fairness in Committee Selection', arXiv:1905.04438) and conjectures 2 is tight. In the approval special case the constant has been driven to 2 ('Sequential Phragmén Guarantees 2-Approximate Core Stability', arXiv:2609.29646) and an exact core is claimed (arXiv:2609.11912), so the open frontier is general monotone and ranking preferences. Related open question from the same section: does an exactly stable lottery exist for all monotone preferences (known only for K <= 3)?

literature.title: Maximum number of stable matchings
literature.statement: A stable-marriage instance of size $n$ has $n$ men and $n$ women, each with a strict total order over all agents of the other side. A perfect matching is stable if no man-woman pair strictly prefer each other to their partners. Let $M(n)$ be the maximum, over all instances of size $n$, of the number of stable matchings. Since $M(a+b)\ge M(a)M(b)$, the limit $\beta=\lim_n M(n)^{1/n}$ exists. Question: determine $\beta$; known $2.28 \lesssim \beta \le 3.55$. In particular, is the classical lower-bound construction (base $\approx 2.28$) optimal?
literature.source_title: At most 3.55^n stable matchings
literature.rationale: One of the classical open questions on stable marriage from the 1970s literature. For decades the best upper bound was super-exponential; 'A Simply Exponential Upper Bound on the Maximum Number of Stable Matchings' (arXiv:1711.01032) gave c^n with a huge constant, and 'At most 3.55^n stable matchings' (arXiv:2011.00915) brought it to 3.55^n via an entropy method. The best lower bound, Omega(2.28^n), comes from a recursive construction for n a power of 2 and has stood since the 1980s. Exact M(n) is known only for small n.

literature.title: Approximately counting stable matchings (FPRAS)
literature.statement: Given a stable-marriage instance with $n$ men and $n$ women having complete strict preferences, let $\#SM$ be its number of stable matchings. Question: is there a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS) for $\#SM$, i.e. a randomized algorithm that, given the instance and $\varepsilon>0$, outputs $Z$ with $\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)\#SM \le Z \le (1+\varepsilon)\#SM]\ge 3/4$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $1/\varepsilon$? This is equivalent (under approximation-preserving reductions) to the existence of an FPRAS for counting independent sets in bipartite graphs (#BIS); it is conjectured that none exists.
literature.source_title: The Complexity of Approximately Counting Stable Matchings
literature.rationale: Exact counting is #P-complete (classical, 1980s). Stable matchings correspond bijectively to downsets (closed sets) of the rotation poset, and every finite poset arises this way, so approximate counting is #BIS-equivalent; 'The Complexity of Approximately Counting Stable Matchings' (arXiv:1004.1836) shows equivalence persists even in restricted attribute models and identifies easy special cases. Resolving it either way would settle the #BIS question, one of the central open problems in approximate counting.

literature.title: Is computing an exact Hylland–Zeckhauser equilibrium FIXP-hard?
literature.statement: A Hylland–Zeckhauser (HZ) market has $n$ agents and $n$ goods, each good with unit supply, and nonnegative utilities $u_{ij}$; every agent has budget 1. An HZ equilibrium is a price vector $p\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n$ and a fractional allocation $x\in[0,1]^{n\times n}$ with $\sum_j x_{ij}=1$ for each agent and $\sum_i x_{ij}=1$ for each good, such that each row $x_i$ maximizes $\sum_j u_{ij}y_j$ over $\{y\ge0: \sum_j y_j=1, \sum_j p_j y_j\le 1\}$ and, among maximizers, minimizes cost $\sum_j p_j y_j$. Equilibria always exist (by a fixed-point argument) but may be irrational. Question: is the problem of computing an exact HZ equilibrium FIXP-hard (hence FIXP-complete, since membership in FIXP is known)?
literature.source_title: Computational Complexity of the Hylland-Zeckhauser Scheme for One-Sided Matching Markets
literature.location: Abstract and Sec. 1 ('We leave open the problem of determining if HZ is FIXP-hard')
literature.rationale: The HZ scheme is the canonical pricing-based mechanism for one-sided matching with cardinal utilities. arXiv:2004.01348 shows equilibria can be irrational and puts the problem in FIXP; 'Computational Hardness of the Hylland-Zeckhauser Scheme' (arXiv:2107.05746) proves PPAD-hardness of computing approximate equilibria (even with 4-valued utilities), settling the approximate case, but leaves exact FIXP-completeness and the 3-valued-utility case open. 'Hardness of approximate Hylland-Zeckhauser equilibria' (arXiv:2606.00951, 2026) extends approximate hardness conditionally. The exact case remains open; few natural market problems are known to be FIXP-complete.

literature.title: Core of simple symmetric fractional hedonic games on bipartite graphs
literature.statement: Let $G=(N,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph. In the associated simple symmetric fractional hedonic game, a partition $\pi$ of $N$ gives each player $i$ utility $u_i(\pi(i)) = |\{j\in \pi(i): \{i,j\}\in E\}| / |\pi(i)|$, where $\pi(i)$ is $i$'s block. A nonempty coalition $S\subseteq N$ blocks $\pi$ if $u_i(S) > u_i(\pi(i))$ for every $i\in S$; $\pi$ is in the core if no coalition blocks it. Question: if $G$ is bipartite, is the core always nonempty?
literature.source_title: Fractional Hedonic Games
literature.rationale: For general simple symmetric fractional hedonic games the core can be empty (a 40-player example in arXiv:1705.10116) and deciding non-emptiness is computationally hard. Non-emptiness is known for graphs of maximum degree at most 2, forests, complete multipartite graphs, graphs of girth at least 5, bipartite graphs with a perfect matching, and regular bipartite graphs; the K_{4,10} example shows star-packing methods that work for girth >= 5 fail for bipartite graphs. Bipartite graphs (girth >= 4) are the natural boundary case. A counterexample would be a finite graph, so computer search plus Lean verification is plausible; a positive proof needs a new idea.

literature.title: Constant-Factor Truthful Mechanism for XOS/Submodular Combinatorial Auctions
literature.statement: There are $n$ bidders and a set $M$ of $m$ items. Each bidder $i$ has a private valuation $v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ with $v_i(\emptyset)=0$. It is monotone and XOS, meaning $v_i(S)=\max_{\ell} \sum_{j\in S} a^{i}_{\ell j}$ for finitely many nonnegative additive clauses $a^i_\ell$. Submodular valuations are a special case. A mechanism learns about valuations only through value queries ($S\mapsto v_i(S)$) and demand queries (prices $p\in\mathbb{R}^M_{\ge0}\mapsto$ some $S\in\arg\max_S v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}p_j$). It may use at most $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)$ queries and computation. It outputs a partition of items to bidders and payments. It is universally truthful if it is a probability distribution over deterministic mechanisms in each of which truthful reporting is a dominant strategy for every bidder. Its approximation ratio is $\sup_{v} \mathrm{OPT}(v)/\mathbb{E}[\sum_i v_i(A_i)]$. Question: is there a universally truthful (or at least truthful-in-expectation) mechanism of this kind whose approximation ratio is $O(1)$, independent of $n$ and $m$? Equivalently, can truthful mechanisms match the constant-factor approximation that non-truthful polynomial-query algorithms achieve?
literature.source_title: Improved Truthful Mechanisms for Subadditive Combinatorial Auctions: Breaking the Logarithmic Barrier
literature.rationale: This is the central open problem on the price of truthfulness in combinatorial auctions. Without incentives, constant factors are easy: $1-1/e$ for XOS with demand queries. Truthful mechanisms went from $O(\log m\log\log m)$ and $O(\sqrt{\log m})$ to $O((\log\log m)^3)$ for submodular/XOS bidders (arXiv:1911.02716) and to $O((\log\log m)^3)$ for subadditive bidders (arXiv:2010.01420). With value queries alone, polynomially many queries provably cannot give better than an $m^{\Omega(1)}$ ratio (see the discussion in arXiv:1911.02716 and 'Limitations of randomized mechanisms for combinatorial auctions', arXiv:1109.1055). The demand-query case is wide open: no super-constant lower bound for truthful mechanisms is known, and no communication separation between truthful mechanisms and algorithms is known either.

literature.title: Optimal Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanism for Unrelated-Machine Scheduling
literature.statement: There are $n$ machines and $m$ jobs. Machine $i$ privately knows its processing times $t_i=(t_{i1},\dots,t_{im})\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^m$. A randomized mechanism maps a reported profile $t$ to a probability distribution over assignments $\sigma:[m]\to[n]$ and to payments $P_i(t)$. Machine $i$'s expected utility is $P_i(t)-\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i} t_{ij}]$ when evaluated at its true times. The mechanism is truthful in expectation (TIE) if no machine can raise its expected utility by misreporting, whatever the others report. Its approximation ratio is $\rho=\sup_t \mathbb{E}_\sigma[\max_i \sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i} t_{ij}] / \mathrm{OPT}(t)$, where $\mathrm{OPT}(t)$ is the minimum makespan. Question: determine $\rho^*_{\mathrm{TIE}}(n)=\inf$ over TIE mechanisms of $\rho$. Is it bounded by a constant, or does it grow linearly in $n$? The case $n=2$ is also open: find the exact optimal ratio for two machines.
literature.source_title: A proof of the Nisan-Ronen conjecture
literature.rationale: The deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture (ratio $n$) was proved in arXiv:2301.11905, so randomization is now the main open question in truthful scheduling. Known bounds: $2-1/n\le\rho^*_{\mathrm{TIE}}(n)\le (n+5)/2$, and fractional mechanisms achieve $(n+1)/2$. For universally truthful mechanisms, 'Universally truthful mechanisms for scheduling' (arXiv:2609.12621) shows a lower bound of $n/12-o(n)$ for discrete-support mechanisms and an upper bound of $n/2+o(n)$. That separates them from the TIE question, which is still open. For $n=2$ the bounds are $1.5$ and about $1.587$ ('Copula-based Randomized Mechanisms for Truthful Scheduling on Two Unrelated Machines', arXiv:1306.3909).

literature.title: Optimal Competitive Ratio for Prophet Secretary
literature.statement: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions $F_1,\dots,F_n$. A uniformly random permutation $\pi$ is drawn and the values are revealed in the order $X_{\pi(1)},X_{\pi(2)},\dots$. After each value is revealed, an online algorithm must irrevocably either stop and receive that value or continue. It may use the distributions, the past values and the identities of the variables seen so far. Let $\alpha^*=\inf_{n,F_1,\dots,F_n}\sup_{\mathrm{ALG}} \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}]/\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]$. Question: determine $\alpha^*$. Known: $0.688\le\alpha^*\le 0.7235$.
literature.source_title: Prophet Secretary
literature.rationale: This is the canonical random-order prophet inequality. It sits between the adversarial-order prophet inequality, where $1/2$ is tight, and the i.i.d. case, where the constant $\approx0.745$ is tight. The original paper (arXiv:1507.01155) gave $1-1/e$. 'Prophet Secretary and Matching: the Significance of the Largest Item' (arXiv:2411.01191) gives $0.688$, beating the $0.675$ barrier for blind strategies. 'Prophet Inequalities: Separating Random Order from Order Selection' (arXiv:2304.04024) gives the upper bound $0.7235$. The gap is still about $0.035$.

literature.title: Free-Order (Order-Selection) Prophet Inequality Constant
literature.statement: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions. Before any value is revealed, the gambler chooses a permutation $\pi$ (it may depend on the distributions). Values $X_{\pi(1)},X_{\pi(2)},\dots$ are then revealed one by one and the gambler stops irrevocably at most once, receiving the current value. Let $\beta^*=\inf_{n,F}\sup_{\pi,\tau}\mathbb{E}[X_{\pi(\tau)}]/\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]$, where $\tau$ ranges over stopping times. Let $\gamma\approx0.7451$ be the i.i.d. prophet constant: the unique $\gamma$ with $\int_0^1 \big(y(1-\ln y)+1/\gamma-1\big)^{-1}dy=1$. Then $\beta^*\le\gamma$. Question: is $\beta^*=\gamma$, i.e., is the worst case for free order attained by i.i.d. instances? Known: $0.7258\le\beta^*\le\gamma$.
literature.source_title: Order Selection Prophet Inequality: From Threshold Optimization to Arrival Time Design
literature.rationale: This is a natural and well-known question: does the power to choose the order fully recover the i.i.d. guarantee? 'Order Selection Prophet Inequality: From Threshold Optimization to Arrival Time Design' (arXiv:2204.01425) raised the lower bound from 0.669 to 0.725. 'Prophet Inequality: Order selection beats random order' (arXiv:2211.04145) gives 0.7258. 'Prophet Inequalities: Separating Random Order from Order Selection' (arXiv:2304.04024) shows random order is strictly worse (at most 0.7235). It is open whether $\beta^*$ equals $\approx0.745$.

literature.title: Exact Approximation Ratio of the Random-Offerer Mechanism
literature.statement: There is one seller with value $s\sim F_S$ and one buyer with value $b\sim F_B$, drawn independently with known distributions on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$. In the seller-offering mechanism, the seller posts $p_S(s)\in\arg\max_p (p-s)(1-F_B(p))$ and trade happens iff $b\ge p_S(s)$. In the buyer-offering mechanism, the buyer posts $p_B(b)\in\arg\max_p (b-p)F_S(p)$ and trade happens iff $s\le p_B(b)$. The random-offerer mechanism (RO) runs each with probability $1/2$. Its gains from trade are $\mathrm{RO}=\mathbb{E}[(b-s)\mathbf 1_{\text{trade}}]$, and $\mathrm{FB}=\mathbb{E}[(b-s)^+]$. Question: determine $R^*=\sup_{F_S,F_B}\mathrm{FB}/\mathrm{RO}$. Known: $2.1728\lesssim R^*\le\pi$. Ties in the argmax may be broken in favour of trade.
literature.source_title: Approximately Efficient Bilateral Trade
literature.rationale: The second-best ratio is now settled at exactly $1/2$ ('Second-Best Bilateral Trade is 1/2 Efficient', arXiv:2606.03849). The tight constant for the simplest dominant-strategy, budget-balanced, IR mechanism is still unknown.
